failed.question:
A suspect was held for questioning at a police station regarding a recent robbery. A police detective advised the suspect of his Miranda rights, which the suspect understood, before asking the suspect about his whereabouts on the night of the robbery. During the questioning, the suspect's attorney called the police station to inform the detective that he was on his way. The detective did not relay this information to the suspect and continued questioning the suspect until he made an incriminating statement. The suspect was subsequently indicted for robbery.
Is the suspect's statement admissible at trial?

A defendant was awaiting trial for his involvement in a fraud scheme that preyed on the elderly. Prior to trial, a reporter called the prosecutor to ask some questions for a news story he was writing on the defendant's upcoming trial. The reporter asked the prosecutor if he was confident that the right person had been apprehended for the fraud scheme. The prosecutor responded, "Well, he would not talk to police without his lawyer, and innocent people speak to the police."
Was the prosecutor's statement proper?

A public defender was appointed by the court to represent an indigent defendant on trial for felony theft. The defendant was offended when the public defender suggested that the defendant consider pleading guilty in light of the evidence against her and the generous plea bargain offered by the prosecution. As a result, the defendant asked the court to appoint another attorney. The court refused but explained that the defendant had the right to dismiss the public defender and proceed pro se. The defendant chose to continue being represented by the public defender. The defendant was subsequently convicted and received a one-year prison sentence that was suspended in full.
Has the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to counsel been violated?

An elementary school teacher detained a student after school. A state prosecutor, alleging that the detention was improper, filed an information charging the teacher with false imprisonment. At trial, the jury rendered a not-guilty verdict.
The student later revealed that on the day of the incident, the teacher had hidden the student in a closet to prevent him from being found. The state prosecutor then filed an information charging the teacher with kidnapping, which requires all of the elements required to establish false imprisonment as well as the movement or hiding of the victim. The teacher, contending that his constitutional rights were violated, has filed a motion to dismiss the charge.
Should the court grant this motion?

A defendant was tried and convicted of murder. The defendant later filed a habeas corpus petition. He contended that because his lawyer at the murder trial had been representing the victim in a criminal charge at the time of the victim's death, the lawyer had a conflict of interest that prevented the defendant from receiving effective assistance of counsel. The lawyer had not revealed this conflict to the trial judge. The trial judge, having no reason to know about the conflict, had not inquired as to whether the lawyer had a conflict of interest that would disqualify her from serving as the defendant's lawyer.
If the defendant's contentions are established and the court overturns the defendant's conviction, what will likely be the reason?

After a defendant was indicted and arraigned on a robbery charge, the defendant was required to participate in a lineup at a police station. The defendant's lawyer was not informed of the lineup, and the defendant did not waive his right to have his lawyer present. At the lineup, the victim of the robbery identified the defendant as the robber.
At trial, the victim again identified the defendant as the robber. When asked about her identification, the victim stated that she was sure the defendant was the robber because she remembered seeing the mole on his right cheek during the robbery. The defendant's lawyer moves to exclude this testimony as obtained in violation of the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
Will the court likely grant this motion?

A defendant was staying at an upscale hotel where he was using his room to run an illegal business. Based on an uncorroborated informant's tip, the police requested that the hotel manager allow them to enter the defendant's room to search for illegal firearms. The manager complied with the request and let the police access the defendant's hotel room without a warrant. Once the police entered the room, they found several illegal firearms that were in plain view.
The defendant was charged with possession of the firearms. He filed a motion to suppress evidence of the firearms prior to trial.
How should the court rule on the defendant's motion to suppress?

One evening, a man called his sister from jail and told her that he had been arrested. The man did not mention retaining a lawyer, so the sister promptly retained a lawyer on the man's behalf. The lawyer contacted the police and demanded to be present when the man was questioned. The police told the lawyer that the man had fallen asleep and would not be questioned until the morning. However, later that evening, the police gave the man Miranda warnings and questioned him for two hours before he voluntarily confessed to the crime. The man never requested a lawyer, and the police did not mention the man's lawyer before or during the interrogation. At his arraignment the next morning, the man was formally charged with robbery.
Should the man's confession be excluded as a violation of his Sixth Amendment right to counsel?

A state prosecutor filed an information charging a man with first-degree arson and first-degree murder. In the applicable jurisdiction, first-degree arson is defined as "the willful and malicious setting fire to and burning of a dwelling."
After the presentation of the prosecution's case, the man's counsel moved for a dismissal of the arson charge because the prosecution had failed to prove that the burned structure was a dwelling. The court granted the motion. However, because the evidence presented by the prosecution established second-degree arson, the court permitted the prosecution to amend the information to charge the man with second-degree arson.
The man then took the stand and, while testifying, admitted that the structure was a dwelling. The court permitted the prosecution to again amend the information to charge the man with first-degree arson. The jury subsequently convicted the man of first-degree arson.
Can the man successfully challenge his conviction on constitutional grounds?

A man was charged with first-degree murder. The prosecutor notified defense counsel that the state would seek the death penalty. Defense counsel filed a motion challenging the prosecution of the man on the ground that he was not mentally competent to stand trial because he has an IQ of 68. After a hearing on the motion, the court concluded that the man was mentally competent to stand trial. The man was subsequently convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death.
When a date was set for the man's execution, defense counsel filed a habeas corpus petition claiming that the man's execution would violate the Eighth Amendment because he is mentally incompetent. A state statute defines an intellectual disability as an IQ of 65 or lower. Current medical guidelines provide that an IQ between 70 and 75 indicates a significant limitation in intellectual functioning, such that an individual within or below that range is presumptively considered to have an intellectual disability.
Should the court allow the man's execution to proceed?

An indigent defendant was tried for misdemeanor assault. The defendant did not request that a lawyer be appointed to represent him, and the court did not appoint one. The crime carries a maximum punishment of one year in prison and a $2,000 fine. The defendant was found guilty, and the court imposed a fine on him.
Has the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to counsel been violated?

The treasurer of a religious charity organization was charged with embezzlement. He received Miranda warnings upon his arrest at work. The treasurer did not respond to questions asked by the two arresting officers during the drive to the police station. When the treasurer and the officers arrived at the police station and began exiting the car, one of the officers asked the treasurer if he could forgive himself for stealing from a charity. The treasurer replied, "No."
At the treasurer's trial, his attorney filed a motion to suppress the treasurer's response to the arresting officer's question.
How should the court rule on the treasurer's motion?

During jury selection at a criminal trial, the defendant used all of his peremptory challenges to strike men from the jury. The prosecution objected to the defendant's actions. The defendant provided a gender-neutral reason for striking the potential male jurors, which the court found to be pretextual.
Was the defendant's use of peremptory challenges unconstitutional?

A defendant, who was represented by a lawyer, was arraigned on a burglary charge and released from custody after posting bail. The defendant's lawyer warned him not to speak to anyone about the case without the lawyer present.
The following day, a police officer approached the defendant outside his apartment building. The officer believed that others, who had not yet been arrested or charged, were also involved in the burglary. The officer asked the defendant if he was willing to discuss the burglary, told him that he was free to decline the request, and read him his Miranda warnings. The defendant thought he could convince the officer that his accomplices were solely responsible for the crime, so he agreed to speak with the officer. During the officer's questioning, the defendant made a statement that implicated him in the burglary.
At trial, the prosecution intends to introduce the defendant's incriminating statement into evidence. The defendant has filed a motion to suppress the statement, contending that it was obtained in violation of his Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
What is the prosecution's best argument that the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to counsel was NOT violated?

Police officers received a report that someone had been murdered. Upon arriving at the scene, a police detective interviewed the only eyewitness to the event. The detective's report, which was delivered to the prosecutor, stated that the eyewitness could not identify the perpetrator of the crime.
A man was subsequently charged with murder. His attorney requested that the prosecution turn over all evidence favorable to the defense. The prosecutor substantially complied with the request but inadvertently failed to disclose the detective's report. At trial, the eyewitness identified the man as the murderer.
The man's attorney learned of the report after the man was convicted. On appeal, the man's attorney argued that the prosecutor's failure to turn over the detective's report violated the man's constitutional rights. He further argued that there was a reasonable probability of a different outcome had the report been disclosed to the defense.
Should the appellate court reverse the man's conviction?

A 17-year-old high school student decided to rob a convenience store. The student entered the store, brandished a pistol, and threatened to shoot the clerk unless she placed the contents of the cash register into a bag. After the clerk emptied the cash register, the student ordered her to lie on the floor and count to 500. To discourage the clerk from moving, the student fired the pistol at the floor immediately beside the clerk. The bullet ricocheted off the floor and struck the clerk in the head, killing her.
The student is now 18 years old and on trial for felony murder.
Can the state constitutionally seek the death penalty?

A man decided to rob a grocery store. During the robbery, he held a store clerk at gunpoint and hit the clerk in the face with the gun before fleeing the store. The police located the store clerk in the hospital the following day. While at the store clerk's bedside, the police officers presented a photo array of possible suspects to the store clerk and went through each photo without making any statements or gestures to him. The store clerk identified the man as the robber, and the man was subsequently arrested. Immediately after his arrest, the man was informed of his Miranda rights. He immediately invoked his right to counsel.
The man has been formally charged with armed robbery. Before trial, the man's attorney filed a motion to exclude the store clerk's identification.
How should the court rule?

A man was arrested and charged with arson. The indictment alleges that the man committed the crime three years ago. The defense has learned that the prosecutor had enough evidence to prosecute the man several months after the arson but made a good-faith decision to delay bringing charges to investigate whether others were involved in the crime. The man contends that the delay has prejudiced his defense because a friend who could have provided the man with an alibi has recently died.
The applicable jurisdiction does not have a statute of limitations regarding arson.
Has the prosecutor's delay violated the man's constitutional rights?

A man sought medical assistance for a gunshot wound to his leg in a hospital emergency room. He told a police officer at the hospital that he had been shot. The officer interviewed the man about the incident while the man was receiving medical treatment. At first, the man stated that he had been shot while attempting to buy drugs on a street corner. However, the discrepancies between the man's wound and his description of the shooting made the officer doubt the veracity of the man's story. The officer knew that the man was unable to leave the hospital due to his injuries, so the officer reminded the man that he did not have to talk with the officer. In response to further questioning, the man revealed that he had shot himself with his own gun.
The man had previously been convicted of a felony, so he was arrested and charged with illegal possession of a firearm by a felon. The man moved to suppress the statement that he had shot himself because he had not been provided with Miranda warnings.
Which of the following standards should the court apply to determine whether the man was in custody for Fifth Amendment purposes?

A police detective sought to question a prisoner, who was serving time for theft, about an unrelated burglary. The prisoner was brought to an interrogation room, and the police detective informed the prisoner of his Miranda rights. The prisoner immediately asserted his right to counsel. The police detective terminated the interview, and the prisoner returned to the normal prison population.
Three weeks later, a different police detective sought to question the prisoner about the same burglary. The detective posed as a prison inmate and engaged the prisoner in a conversation designed to elicit details about the burglary. The prisoner confessed to his involvement in the burglary during the detective's questioning. The prisoner was subsequently charged with burglary.
The prosecution seeks to introduce the prisoner's confession at the burglary trial. The prisoner's attorney has objected.
Is the prisoner's confession admissible?

Police received an anonymous tip that a gardener was growing marijuana in her backyard, which was surrounded by a 15-foot-high, solid wooden fence. A police officer was unable to view the yard from the street, so he used a police helicopter to fly over the gardener's house at a height of 1,000 feet. The officer identified a large patch of marijuana plants growing right next to the house and used this observation to obtain a search warrant.
The gardener is prosecuted for possession of marijuana and moves to suppress use of the marijuana in evidence.
How should the court rule on the gardener's motion?
